title: More SQL commands: ALTER, CASE, UNION, VIEW, and UPSERT

spans.text: “More SQL commands: ALTER, CASE, UNION, VIEW, and UPSERT” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
The query returns a price group; on conflict, the product with that unique key is updated.

SQL statements can be grouped by purpose: DDL defines schema (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML changes data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL queries it (SELECT), TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK), and DCL manages permissions (GRANT, REVOKE). ALTER TABLE changes an existing table; CASE chooses a value by condition; UNION combines results and removes duplicates, while UNION ALL preserves them. A VIEW names a saved SELECT query without copying the data. UPSERT inserts or updates on a unique-key conflict. Database creation and upsert syntax vary by DBMS: MySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, while SQLite and PostgreSQL use `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`. Triggers run automatically after INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE and should be used carefully because they can hide side effects.

Key line: `-- MySQL:`
What it does: The schema gains a column; CASE assigns a category; UNION ALL combines results; VIEW names a reusable query; UPSERT updates on conflict.
Why it is used: Test schema changes on a disposable database first; do not assume dialect portability without checking the target DBMS.
If omitted or changed: SQLite/PostgreSQL use `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` for upserts; the MySQL equivalent is `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`.

spans.title: Common mistake
spans.text: DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, and triggers can remove or automatically change data; understand the effect and keep a backup.
